label: copy-phase input token x
explanation: Fires only when the token x is fed back as an input during the copy phase (t > L), i.e. when the model just output an x it is copying. It never fires on x in the original phase, on the delimiter, or on any other token; every activation is covered by the predicate (dev recall 1.0). About 22% of copy-phase x inputs are inactive or near zero, scattered across positions, with no clean distinguishing condition (excluding the first copy step or late steps lowers F1). Magnitude: the top examples are usually the first x of a run of x inputs, and an immediately following second x is weaker (about 0.1-0.5 of max). Rate is slightly lower at early recall positions, and sequences that start with x are over-represented.

issues: The core predicate holds. On both dev and test, (phase==2)&(in_tok==x) catches every activation (recall 1.0, 0 missed activations). The feature never fires in the original phase, on the delimiter step, or on any other token.

The explanation says no clean condition separates the misses. That is wrong: the misses depend systematically on out_tok, the token being output at the same step (the original token right after the x). On dev, the firing rate within the predicate is 0.35 for out_tok=j, 0.32 for k, 0.50 for a, 0.55 for b and 0.58 for p. It is 0.99 for out_tok=x (0.998 on test) and over 0.93 for e, g, l, n, o. Test: x followed by j or k has precision 0.33.

The magnitude claim is attributed to the wrong cause. The explanation says the first x in a run is strongest and an x right after another x is weaker. On test, prev_tok==x has a firing rate of 0.75 (base rate 0.78), and its mass recall per unit of recall is 0.024/0.026, about 0.93x the average. So an x after an x is barely weaker than average. What actually drives magnitude is out_tok==x: mass recall 0.088 against recall 0.042, about 2.1x the average activation, and precision about 1.0. The top examples are first-of-pair x's because the next output is also x.

'Sequences that start with x are over-represented' is misleading. Their rate per step is higher only because those sequences contain more x tokens. Among copy-phase x inputs, first_tok==x actually has a lower firing rate (precision 0.70 against 0.78).

Smaller points that check out: precision at recall_idx==1 is 0.70, so the rate is lower at early recall positions. Restricting to recall_idx>=2 does lower F1 (about 0.82). The feature fires more on the last copy step (to_go==0, precision 0.87) and in short sequences (L<=5, precision 0.89). These are modest effects.
Excluding out_tok in {j,k} raises test F1 only from 0.877 to 0.885. So the label is fine, but the explanation's claims about misses and magnitude need correcting.
